chapter_title: The Iterator Pattern: Traversing Collections Gracefully

screens.title: The Iterator Pattern
screens.subtitle: Traversing collections without exposing their internals

narration.text: In this chapter we explore the Iterator pattern and why it matters when working with collections. The Iterator pattern gives clients a uniform way to traverse an aggregate object sequentially without revealing how that aggregate stores data. That matters because it keeps traversal logic decoupled from storage choices. For example, a BookShelf might be backed by an array today and a linked list tomorrow; with an iterator, client code that prints book titles does not change. You'll also learn the difference between external iterators, where the client controls stepping with hasNext and next, and internal iterators, where the collection applies a callback or stream operation. We'll walk through a concrete Java BookShelf example, show a safe inner-class iterator implementation, and highlight the common concurrent-modification pitfall and strategies to handle it. By the end of this lesson you will be able to design custom iterators for your own aggregates, understand when to prefer internal iteration for simplicity, and how iterator design supports single responsibility and maintainability. Consider how traversal responsibilities split between collection and iterator as you move forward.

keyIdea.title: Core Insight
keyIdea.text: Iterator separates traversal from storage so clients traverse uniformly while the aggregate controls representation and safety.

content.html:

Aggregate

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will have four practical skills. First, you will be able to explain the purpose and benefits of the Iterator pattern: why separating traversal from storage reduces coupling and increases flexibility. For example, you will be able to justify replacing an array with a linked list inside an aggregate without changing client traversal code. Second, you will implement the Iterator pattern in Java for a custom aggregate, providing hasNext and next in a concrete iterator and using an inner class to access aggregate state safely. Third, you will differentiate internal versus external iteration, recognizing when a callback-based forEach or a stream is more convenient than giving the client explicit step control. Finally, you will identify common scenarios where iterators simplify code—such as playlists, bookshelves, and tree traversals—and you will handle concurrent modification concerns by choosing fail-fast checks or constraining modification. Each objective maps to a verified competency milestone so you can measure your progress and practice with the provided hands-on Playlist activity.

screens.title: How We'll Practice
screens.subtitle: Skills, examples, and safety checks to practice with code

narration.text: This second objectives slide focuses on practice and safety. You will implement a concrete BookShelf iterator and a Playlist iterator so you can see inner-class iterators accessing aggregate state. The recommended approach is to make the iterator an inner class so it can see private fields like an internal array or linked list, which simplifies tracking an index or node pointer. You will also practice a simple safety measure: when your iterator is created, capture a modification count and compare it on each step. If a change is detected, throw an exception to avoid silently corrupting traversal results. Finally, you will reflect on when to prefer internal iteration: operations that map, filter, or aggregate are often simpler and may perform better when the aggregate controls traversal. Each practice item maps to a small test: print titles, detect concurrent modifications, and add an Iterable interface to enable the enhanced for-loop. These tasks build both coding skill and design judgment.

screens.title: What the Iterator Pattern Is
screens.subtitle: Definition, purpose, and a simple mental model

narration.text: The Iterator pattern defines a way to access elements of an aggregate sequentially without exposing its underlying representation. In plain terms, it moves the responsibility for stepping through elements out of the collection and into a separate object that knows how to traverse. This gives a predictable walk protocol—usually hasNext() and next()—so clients can read items in order without learning internal details like array positions or node pointers. For a concrete mental model, imagine a conveyor belt inside a factory boxed away from customers; the customer asks an attendant for the next item but never sees the belt mechanics. The pattern matters because it reduces coupling: clients depend on the traversal contract, not on storage details, so you can change the aggregate’s implementation later without changing client code. A common misconception is that iterators duplicate collection responsibility; they do not. The iterator's only job is traversal, while the aggregate continues to manage element storage and lifecycle. Example: a BookShelf may expose createIterator(), and the returned iterator yields Book objects using hasNext and next. Takeaway: treat traversal as a focused role, remove traversal logic from clients, and prefer an inner-class iterator when it needs direct access to private state.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Iterator provides a traversal interface so clients iterate without accessing internal structure.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › What the Iterator Pattern Is
Definition
Iterator: an object that steps through an aggregate sequentially

Treat traversal as a single responsibility. The aggregate manages data; the iterator manages traversal.

Analogy

Think of an attendant delivering items from a concealed conveyor belt — the customer never sees the mechanism.

Key Takeaway

Separate traversal responsibilities to make collections easier to change and reuse.

Concrete Example (conceptual)
BookShelf
Provides createIterator() which returns a BookIterator that knows how to walk shelf positions.
Playlist
ConcretePlaylist returns PlaylistIterator that traverses an internal linked list of songs.
Common misconception

Iterators do not duplicate collection responsibilities. They only observe or step through elements; they should not manage element lifecycle or storage policies.

narration.text: Let's walk through the canonical BookShelf example to see how interfaces define roles. Start with the iterator interface that declares hasNext and next. Then define an aggregate interface with a factory method createIterator, so clients ask the aggregate for an iterator rather than touching internals. The Book class holds title and author fields and exposes simple accessors; it is the element type yielded by the iterator. Implementing a concrete aggregate like ConcreteBookShelf gives you an internal storage—an array in the example—and a method to add books. The createIterator implementation returns a Concrete Iterator, often implemented as an inner class. An inner-class iterator can directly access the aggregate's private fields like the internal array and length index. That simplifies implementation and avoids exposing getters just for iteration. A concrete iterator keeps a traversal index and increments it on each next call, and throws a NoSuchElementException when no elements remain. This pattern keeps client code very simple: create the aggregate, add elements, ask for an iterator, then loop with hasNext and next. One practical question: how will you record modifications so the iterator can detect concurrent changes? We'll address that next.

keyIdea.title: Role Checklist
keyIdea.text: Iterator: traversal; Aggregate: storage and iterator factory; Element: simple data holder (Book or Song).

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › BookShelf Example
Interfaces and Element
// BookIterator
interface BookIterator {
  boolean hasNext();
  Book next();
}

// BookShelfAggregate
interface BookShelfAggregate {
  BookIterator createIterator();
}

// Book (element)
class Book {
  private String title;
  private String author;
  public Book(String title, String author) { this.title = title; this.author = author; }
  public String getTitle() { return title; }
  public String getAuthor() { return author; }
}
Conceptual diagram
ConcreteBookShelf stores an array and returns BookShelfIterator
BookShelfIterator keeps an index, calls getBookAt(index) and increments
Client obtains iterator and loops with hasNext()/next()
Common mistake

Exposing internal collection for clients to iterate directly creates tight coupling and fragile code.

screens.title: ConcreteBookShelf: Inner Class Iterator
screens.subtitle: How the iterator accesses private state and manages traversal

narration.text: Now we focus on the concrete implementation in which the iterator is an inner class. Implement ConcreteBookShelf with a private Book[] array and a lastAdded index that tracks the number of books. The createIterator method simply returns a new iterator instance. The inner class BookShelfIterator keeps an index that starts at zero and uses the aggregate's getLength and getBookAt methods or direct field access to retrieve items. When next is called, the iterator checks hasNext and either returns the book and increments index, or throws a NoSuchElementException if there are no more items. Making the iterator an inner class is convenient because it can see private members without adding public getters solely for iteration. That keeps the aggregate's A P I minimal. One important design choice is whether to allow modifications while iterating. For many simple custom collections the practical approach is to record a modification counter on the aggregate and have the iterator check it on each step, failing fast if it changes. Alternatively, you may prohibit modification methods while iteration is active. The inner-class pattern plus a modCount check gives a clear and maintainable implementation.

keyIdea.title: Inner-class benefit
keyIdea.text: Inner-class iterators access private aggregate state directly, keeping the aggregate API clean while enabling efficient traversal.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › ConcreteBookShelf: Inner Class Iterator
Concrete aggregate snippet
class ConcreteBookShelf implements BookShelfAggregate {
  private Book[] books;
  private int lastAdded = 0;
  private int modCount = 0; // simple modification counter

  public ConcreteBookShelf(int maxSize) {
    this.books = new Book[maxSize];
  }

  public void addBook(Book book) {
    if (lastAdded < books.length) {
      books[lastAdded++] = book;
      modCount++;
    }
  }

  public BookIterator createIterator() { return new BookShelfIterator(); }

  private class BookShelfIterator implements BookIterator {
    private int index = 0;
    private final int expectedMod = modCount;

    public boolean hasNext() { return index < lastAdded; }

    public Book next() {
      if (expectedMod != modCount) throw new java.util.ConcurrentModificationException();
      if (!hasNext()) throw new java.util.NoSuchElementException();
      return books[index++];
    }
  }
}
Explanation cards
modCount pattern: capture on creation, verify each next(), throw on mismatch to fail fast.
NoSuchElementException: defensive check when client calls next() but no elements remain.
Inner class access: allows iterator to reach private books[] and lastAdded directly without extra getters.
Pro tip

Keep iterator responsibility narrow: step and return. Avoid mutation logic in next().

narration.text: Understanding the difference between external and internal iterators helps you choose the right approach. An external iterator—like Java's Iterator interface—gives the client control. The client calls hasNext and next, which makes complex traversal logic, early returns, or conditional stepping straightforward. For example, a client can stop after finding a matching book, or traverse only every other element if needed. The downside is repeated method calls and slightly more boilerplate. An internal iterator encapsulates the traversal inside the aggregate: the collection takes a callback or exposes forEach/stream operations and applies the function to each element. This is often simpler for straightforward transformations and can be more performant because the aggregate controls iteration overhead and can optimize. A common misconception is that internal iteration is always better because it is terse; instead, choose internal iteration when you need simple element-wise operations and prefer external iteration when clients need stepping control, complex traversal order, or to maintain external state across steps. Consider both A P I ergonomics and performance trade-offs when designing your aggregate. External vs Internal Iterators means external iteration for client control; internal iteration for simplicity and potential optimizations.. In practical terms, client-controlled stepping versus aggregate-controlled callbacks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Trade-off
keyIdea.text: External iteration for client control; internal iteration for simplicity and potential optimizations.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › External vs Internal Iterators
External Iterator (explicit)
  • Client calls hasNext() and next() to control stepping.
  • Good for complex traversal, early exit, or conditional steps.
  • Slightly more verbose; method-call overhead per element.
Internal Iterator (callback)
  • Aggregate applies a callback or exposes forEach/stream operations.
  • Simpler for mapping, filtering, and aggregation; aggregate can optimize.
  • Less control for client; not ideal for irregular stepping or complex stateful traversal.
Scenario guide
Use external iterator when you need to pause, rewind, or take different actions based on element position.
Use internal iteration for simple pipelines like print, map, or sum where the aggregate can control traversal efficiently.
Hybrid: provide both APIs so clients choose the most appropriate one.
Check your understanding

Can the client stop early? If yes, prefer external iteration; if not and operations are uniform, internal is fine.

screens.title: Design Steps for a Custom Iterator
screens.subtitle: A checklist to implement an iterator safely in Java

narration.text: When implementing a custom iterator, follow a deliberate process to keep behavior clear and robust. Step one: define the minimal iterator interface—hasNext and next—targeted to your element type. Step two: design the aggregate interface that exposes a factory method createIterator; avoid exposing internal collections as public fields. Step three: choose whether your concrete iterator should be an inner class; inner classes simplify access to private state and are a common, practical choice in Java. Step four: decide how to handle concurrent modification. A simple and effective approach is to maintain a modCount on the aggregate, increment it for mutations, and capture its value in the iterator at creation; the iterator then checks this expected count on each next call and throws a ConcurrentModificationException if it sees a mismatch. Step five: add defensive checks such as throwing NoSuchElementException when next is called without a next element. Finally, step six: consider adding Iterable support so clients can use the enhanced for-loop, returning a java. util. Iterator if you want standard interoperability. Following these steps reduces bugs and makes the iterator predictable for clients.

keyIdea.title: Implementation Checklist
keyIdea.text: Define interfaces, prefer inner-class iterators, add modCount checks, and provide Iterable when useful.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Design Steps for a Custom Iterator
Step-by-step
1.
Define iterator and aggregate interfaces.
2.
Implement concrete aggregate with private storage and add methods to mutate safely.
3.
Implement iterator as inner class and maintain traversal index or node pointer.
4.
Add modCount checks to detect concurrent modification or choose to disallow mutations during iteration.
5.
Expose Iterable to enable enhanced for-loop if interoperability is desired.
Example scenario
Playlist backed by LinkedList<Song> where PlaylistIterator keeps an index or node reference and checks expectedMod each step.
Key Takeaway

A clear checklist reduces subtle bugs and clarifies who owns traversal responsibility.

screens.title: Supporting Java's Enhanced For-Loop
screens.subtitle: Implementing Iterable to interoperate with language features

narration.text: Java's enhanced for-loop is syntactic sugar that depends on an object implementing Iterable. If you want clients to write for (Book book : bookShelf) you must implement java. lang. Iterable and return a java. util. Iterator from iterator(). This interoperable approach maps directly to the Iterator pattern: your concrete iterator can still be an inner class, but it should implement java. util. Iterator to satisfy the language contract. The benefit is ergonomic: clients use concise loops and library utilities expect Iterable. The trade-off is that you tie the aggregate to Java's standard interfaces, which is usually desirable. When implementing iterator(), create and return a new iterator instance each time so multiple clients can iterate concurrently without interfering with one another. If your aggregate is mutable, ensure your iterator captures expected modCount to detect concurrent modifications. Example: make ConcreteBookShelf implement Iterable and have iterator() return new BookShelfIterator(); this allows both manual external iteration and the enhanced for-loop. The core idea remains: provide a stable traversal A P I so client code stays simple regardless of internal changes. Supporting Java's Enhanced For-Loop means implement iterable and return a java.util.iterator to enable the enhanced for-loop and standard library compatibility.. In practical terms, implementing iterable to interoperate with language features. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Interoperability
keyIdea.text: Implement Iterable and return a java.util.Iterator to enable the enhanced for-loop and standard library compatibility.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Supporting Enhanced For-Loop
Implement Iterable
class ConcreteBookShelf implements Iterable<Book> {
  // existing fields and methods
  @Override
  public java.util.Iterator<Book> iterator() {
    return new BookShelfIterator(); // inner class that implements java.util.Iterator
  }
}

// Now client can do:
// for (Book book : bookShelf) { System.out.println(book.getTitle()); }
Notes
Return a fresh iterator for each call to iterator() so iterations are independent.
Use java.util.Iterator methods to integrate with libraries and language constructs.
If you expose both a custom iterator and Iterable, document the expectations about concurrent modification behavior.

screens.title: Concurrent Modification: Pitfalls and Strategies
screens.subtitle: Why fail-fast exists and how to adopt a practical strategy

narration.text: Concurrent modification during iteration is a frequent source of bugs. When a client holds an external iterator and another thread or part of the code mutates the aggregate—adding or removing elements—the iterator's internal position can become invalid. In Java's standard library, many collections implement fail-fast iterators by maintaining a modification count on the collection and comparing it with an expected value captured by the iterator. If they differ, the iterator throws ConcurrentModificationException to alert the developer immediately. When implementing your own aggregate, you must choose a strategy: disallow mutation during iteration, implement modCount checks and fail-fast behavior, or design a fully concurrent iterator that can tolerate mutations (which is complex). For beginner-level custom collections, the modCount approach is pragmatic: increment modCount on mutating methods, capture it on iterator creation, and verify it inside next. Remember that fail-fast is not a substitute for correct concurrent design: it detects unexpected mutations but does not guarantee thread safety. The takeaway is to pick the simplest safe choice for your needs and document the iterator’s behavior so clients know whether mutation during iteration is supported.

keyIdea.title: Safety Strategy
keyIdea.text: Use a modCount and fail-fast checks to detect modification during iteration or explicitly disallow concurrent mutations.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Concurrent Modification
Fail-fast pattern
// On aggregate
private int modCount = 0;
public void add(Book b) { /* add */ modCount++; }
public void remove(Book b) { /* remove */ modCount++; }

// In iterator
private final int expected = modCount;
public Book next() {
  if (expected != modCount) throw new java.util.ConcurrentModificationException();
  // proceed
}
Alternatives and notes
Disallow mutations: simplest but restrictive; throw on mutating methods when iteration is active.
Concurrent iterators: implement snapshot iterators that iterate over a copy to avoid exceptions at cost of memory.
Document the chosen behavior so clients understand whether iteration is fail-fast, snapshot-based, or thread-safe.
Misconception check

Fail-fast does not make your collection thread-safe; it only detects unexpected concurrent changes and fails early.

screens.title: Playlist Lab: Starter Code and Expectations
screens.subtitle: Implement a ConcretePlaylist with PlaylistIterator (LinkedList backing)

narration.text: This hands-on lab asks you to implement a ConcretePlaylist that uses java. util. LinkedList<Song> internally and a PlaylistIterator inner class. The Song class is a simple data holder with title and artist properties. Define SongIterator with hasNext and next. Make PlaylistAggregate define createIterator and addSong. ConcretePlaylist will keep songs as a LinkedList, add songs via addSong, and return a new PlaylistIterator from createIterator. The iterator can track an index or a java. util. ListIterator internally; for clarity in the starter code we use an index-based approach that calls songs. get(index++). Remember to throw NoSuchElementException when next is called with no remaining elements. To increase safety, capture an expected modification count so the iterator can detect unexpected changes. In the main method, create the playlist, add a few songs, then obtain the iterator and print each song via iterator. next until hasNext returns false. This lab is intentionally small: it focuses on A P I design, inner-class convenience, and the modCount safety pattern. Write small tests: print titles, modify the playlist during iteration to see the exception, and optionally make ConcretePlaylist implement Iterable to use the enhanced for-loop.

screens.title: Assessing Iterator Design for Trees
screens.subtitle: How to provide multiple traversal orders for a BinaryTree

narration.text: Consider a BinaryTree that stores Node objects and you need pre-order, in-order, and post-order traversals. The Iterator pattern fits well: define a TreeIterator interface with hasNext and next, or reuse java. util. Iterator<Node>. Define a TreeAggregate with createIterator that accepts a TraversalType parameter. The aggregate's createIterator can return different concrete iterator implementations: PreOrderIterator, InOrderIterator, and PostOrderIterator. Each concrete iterator encapsulates traversal state—often an explicit stack for non-recursive traversal—or uses a controlled recursion-preserving structure so next() returns the next node in the chosen order. This design prevents exposing Node internals to clients and keeps traversal implementations isolated. A common pitfall is failing to manage recursion state correctly across calls to next; iterative implementations typically use a stack to represent pending nodes. For mutable trees, consider whether iterators should be fail-fast by tracking structural modification counts. This design allows clients to request the desired traversal order and iterate uniformly without learning tree internals. Try sketching interfaces and at least one concrete iterator to solidify these ideas. Assessing Iterator Design for Trees means return different concrete iterators for each traversal order to hide tree structure and provide uniform iteration apis.. In practical terms, how to provide multiple traversal orders for a binarytree. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Tree Traversal
keyIdea.text: Return different concrete iterators for each traversal order to hide tree structure and provide uniform iteration APIs.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Assessing Iterator Design for Trees
Interface sketch
enum TraversalType { PRE_ORDER, IN_ORDER, POST_ORDER }

interface TreeIterator { boolean hasNext(); Node next(); }

interface TreeAggregate { TreeIterator createIterator(TraversalType type); }
Design notes
Each concrete iterator encapsulates traversal state such as a stack for iterative traversal.
Keep traversal logic isolated so clients never touch nodes directly.
For mutable trees consider modCount checks to provide fail-fast behavior when needed.
Assessment prompt

screens.title: Design Guidelines and Common Mistakes
screens.subtitle: Maintain separation of concerns and document iterator behavior

narration.text: As you design iterators, follow a handful of best practices to avoid frequent mistakes. First, keep iterator responsibilities narrow: stepping and returning elements only. Do not mix mutation of the collection into next or hasNext. Second, prefer inner-class iterators when they need direct access to private state; this avoids exposing getters that serve only iteration. Third, choose and document your concurrent modification strategy—fail-fast, snapshot, or disallowing mutation—so clients know what to expect. Fourth, return a fresh iterator for each call to iterator() so multiple iterations do not interfere. Common mistakes include exposing internal collections publicly, which couples clients to representation; forgetting to check bounds and throwing NoSuchElementException; and assuming fail-fast provides thread safety. Another frequent oversight is failing to consider the cost of internal iteration vs external iteration: libraries and streams can optimize internal iteration, but you sacrifice fine-grained control. The practical guideline is to provide a clear A P I, choose a default strategy consistent with the rest of your codebase, and include unit tests that exercise normal iteration, early exit, and concurrent modification detection. Design Guidelines and Common Mistakes means keep iterators focused, prefer inner classes for access, document concurrent-modification behavior, and return fresh iterators.. In practical terms, maintain separation of concerns and document iterator behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Best Practices
keyIdea.text: Keep iterators focused, prefer inner classes for access, document concurrent-modification behavior, and return fresh iterators.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Design Guidelines and Common Mistakes
Guidelines
  • Separate traversal from storage; iterator only steps and returns elements.
  • Use inner-class iterators for direct access to private state, keeping the public API small.
  • Implement modCount checks or snapshot behavior and document which you choose.
  • Return a new iterator for each iterator() invocation so iterations are independent.
  • Write unit tests for normal iteration, edge cases, and concurrent modification detection.
Common mistakes
Exposing internal collections publicly which creates fragile client code.
Not checking bounds and letting next() return null instead of throwing NoSuchElementException.
Assuming fail-fast equals thread-safety; it only detects unexpected changes.

narration.text: To summarize, the Iterator pattern provides a uniform traversal protocol that hides the aggregate’s internal structure. The aggregate manages storage and exposes a factory method to create iterators, while the iterator implements stepping methods such as hasNext and next. Use inner-class iterators in Java to access private fields directly, and consider adding a modification counter to implement fail-fast detection of concurrent changes. Decide between external iteration when clients need control and internal iteration for simple, often optimized pipelines. Finally, implement Iterable when you want clients to use the enhanced for-loop and keep iterator responsibilities narrow and well-tested. These guidelines will help your collections remain flexible, testable, and safe to use in larger systems. Key Concepts means iterator = traversal contract; aggregate = storage + iterator factory; choose iteration style and safety policy consciously.. In practical terms, what to remember. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Essentials
keyIdea.text: Iterator = traversal contract; Aggregate = storage + iterator factory; choose iteration style and safety policy consciously.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Key Concepts
Iterator
An object that exposes hasNext and next to traverse elements sequentially.
Aggregate
The collection that stores elements and provides createIterator.
Internal vs External
External: client-controlled stepping. Internal: aggregate applies a callback or stream operation.
Summary takeaway

Design iterators to be simple, document mutation policies, and prefer inner-class iterators in Java when they need aggregate access.

narration.text: Keep three compact reminders in mind: define a clear traversal contract so clients don't rely on implementation details; choose internal or external iteration based on control needs and simplicity; and adopt a consistent safety policy for concurrent modification such as modCount-based fail-fast checks or snapshot iterators. These rules will guide practical, maintainable iterator implementations in Java and help your code remain robust as internal data structures evolve. Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › What to Remember
Define the contract
hasNext and next should be the reliable API clients depend on.
Choose iteration style
External for control; internal for simple pipelines and potential optimizations.
Adopt a safety policy
Use modCount fail-fast or snapshot strategies and document the choice.
Final takeaway

A clear traversal API and a simple safety approach make iterators reliable and your collections easier to evolve.
